title: Osteology of the Upper Limb
introduction: The upper limb skeleton comprises the shoulder region (scapula and clavicle), the arm (humerus), the forearm (ulna and radius), and the wrist and hand (carpal bones, metacarpals, and phalanges)[cite: 161, 165]. Understanding bony landmarks, joint articulations, and closely related neurovascular structures is essential for diagnosing upper limb fractures and nerve injuries[cite: 167, 174, 187].
learningOutcomes: 1.1 Identify the bony landmarks, surfaces, and muscular attachments of the scapula and clavicle[cite: 162, 163, 166].
1.2 Explain the functions, neurovascular relations, and common fracture sites of the clavicle[cite: 167, 168, 169].
1.3 Describe the anatomy of the humerus and match humeral fracture sites to their vulnerable nerves[cite: 170, 171, 172, 174].
1.4 Differentiate the structural features of the ulna and radius and classify key forearm and wrist fractures[cite: 176, 178, 184, 187].
1.5 Name the carpal bones, carpal arch boundaries, hand bones, and clinical risks such as scaphoid avascular necrosis and carpal tunnel syndrome[cite: 189, 190, 192, 193, 194, 195].

content.heading: The Scapula
content.body: The scapula is a triangular bone on the posterolateral aspect of the thorax overlying the 2nd to 7th ribs[cite: 162]. Its three prominent features are the glenoid cavity (fossa) laterally for the shoulder joint, the posterior spine projecting laterally as the acromion process, and the anterior coracoid process[cite: 162]. The costal (ventral) surface forms the concave subscapular fossa, whose medial two-thirds provide attachment for the subscapularis[cite: 163]. The dorsal surface is divided by the spine into the supraspinatous fossa (containing supraspinatus) and infraspinatous fossa (containing infraspinatus)[cite: 163]. Because strong muscles cover both sides, the scapula is rarely fractured except by severe direct violence (such as pedestrian vehicle accidents), usually alongside rib fractures, with most scapular fractures involving the protruding acromion[cite: 164].

content.heading: The Clavicle (Collar Bone)
content.body: The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle, sits nearly horizontally above the first rib, and has no medullary cavity[cite: 165, 166]. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula[cite: 165]. Its flat upper surface provides attachment for the deltoid anteriorly and the trapezius posteriorly[cite: 166]. Posterior to the medial third of the shaft pass the third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle[cite: 167]. Behind the sternoclavicular joints lie the left common carotid artery on the left, the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, and the internal jugular vein laterally on both sides, separated by the sternohyoid and sternothyroid strap muscles[cite: 167, 168]. The clavicle has three functions: transmitting forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, acting as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by the trapezius), and providing muscle attachments[cite: 168]. It is one of the most frequently fractured bones; its weakest point is the junction of the middle and outer third, commonly broken by indirect force from falls on the shoulder or hand[cite: 169].

content.heading: The Humerus & Vulnerable Nerves
content.body: The humerus is the longest and largest bone of the upper limb[cite: 170]. Its proximal end has a rounded head, anatomical neck, and greater and lesser tubercles separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which lodges the long tendon of biceps brachii and transmits a branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery[cite: 170]. The narrow surgical neck lies where the upper end meets the shaft, in direct contact with the axillary nerve and circumflex humeral vessels[cite: 170]. The posterior shaft bears the spiral (radial) groove separating the medial and lateral heads of triceps, where the radial nerve and profunda vessels wind[cite: 171]. Distally, the rounded capitulum articulates laterally with the radial head, and the spool-shaped trochlea articulates medially with the trochlear notch of the ulna[cite: 172]. The medial epicondyle is larger than the lateral epicondyle, extends farther distally, and has a posterior groove for the ulnar nerve[cite: 172]. Fractures threaten specific nerves by location: surgical neck fractures endanger the axillary nerve (especially common in elderly patients with osteoporosis after a minor fall on the hand), midshaft radial groove fractures endanger the radial nerve, distal/supracondylar fractures endanger the median nerve, and medial epicondyle fractures endanger the ulnar nerve[cite: 174, 175].

content.heading: The Ulna & Radius
content.body: The ulna is the medial, longer, stabilizing bone of the forearm[cite: 176]. Its proximal end features the olecranon posteriorly and coronoid process anteriorly, forming the trochlear notch that articulates with the humeral trochlea[cite: 176]. The ulna tapers distally to a rounded head and conical ulnar styloid process and does not participate in the wrist (radiocarpal) joint[cite: 177]. The radius is the lateral, shorter forearm bone[cite: 178]. Its proximal end comprises a cylindrical head (concave superiorly to articulate with the humeral capitulum, and articulating medially with the radial notch of the ulna), a short neck, and the medial radial tuberosity[cite: 178]. The radial shaft enlarges distally, forming the medial ulnar notch (for the ulnar head) and terminating laterally as the radial styloid process, which is larger and extends farther distally than the ulnar styloid process[cite: 179].

content.heading: Clinical Fractures of the Forearm & Elbow
content.body: Because pronator teres inserts midway along the radial shaft, fractures proximal to it leave the proximal fragment supinated by the biceps and the distal fragment pronated by pronator teres, requiring splinting in supination; fractures distal to the midshaft are balanced and immobilized in a neutral position[cite: 182]. A fall on an outstretched hand produces age-dependent injuries: posterior displacement of the distal radial epiphysis in children, radial/ulnar shaft or scaphoid fractures in young adults, and Colles' fracture in the elderly[cite: 183]. In a Colles' fracture, the radius breaks about 2.5 cm proximal to the wrist with dorsal (posterior) displacement and impaction, producing a dinner fork deformity and bringing the radial and ulnar styloid processes in line[cite: 184, 187]. Other specific fractures include Smith's fracture (distal radius fracture with volar/ventral displacement), Galeazzi fracture (radius fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation), Monteggia fracture (proximal third ulna fracture with radial head dislocation), and Essex-Lopresti fracture (radial head fracture with distal radioulnar dislocation and interosseous membrane disruption)[cite: 187]. Falls on an outstretched hand can also crush the radial head against the capitulum, while the olecranon may be avulsed by forcible triceps contraction (requiring operative repair)[cite: 185]. Repeated trauma over the subcutaneous olecranon bursa causes olecranon bursitis, known as student's elbow or miner's elbow[cite: 186].

content.heading: Bones of the Wrist (Carpus) & Hand
content.body: The wrist (carpus) contains 8 carpal bones arranged in two rows of four, with the proximal row articulating with the distal radius and the articular disc of the wrist joint[cite: 188]. From lateral to medial, the proximal row consists of the scaphoid (boat-shaped with a tubercle), lunate (moon-shaped, broader anteriorly), triquetrum (pyramidal), and pisiform (pea-shaped on the palmar surface of the triquetrum)[cite: 189]. The distal row consists of the trapezium (four-sided), trapezoid (wedge-shaped), capitate (head-shaped and largest carpal bone), and hamate (wedge-shaped with an anterior hook)[cite: 190]. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone after a fall on an outstretched hand and is at high risk of avascular necrosis because only one small artery enters near its thumb-side end[cite: 191, 192]. The carpal bones form an anteriorly concave carpal arch bounded laterally by the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the pisiform and hook of hamate[cite: 193]. The flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) roofs this arch to form the carpal tunnel, housing the long flexor tendons and the median nerve; compression of the median nerve causes carpal tunnel syndrome (paraesthesiae, numbness, and motor weakness), relieved by longitudinally dividing the retinaculum[cite: 194]. Distally, the hand contains 19 bones (5 metacarpals in the palm and 14 phalanges—3 per finger and 2 in the thumb) forming 14 synovial joints, including the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) knuckle joints and interphalangeal (IP) joints[cite: 195, 196].

inTextQuestions.question: Which part of the clavicle is its weakest point and most frequent site of fracture?
inTextQuestions.answer: The junction of the middle and outer third[cite: 169].

inTextQuestions.question: Which nerve winds through the spiral (radial) groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus?
inTextQuestions.answer: The radial nerve (accompanied by the profunda vessels)[cite: 171].

inTextQuestions.question: Does the ulna participate in the wrist (radiocarpal) joint?
inTextQuestions.answer: No, the ulna does not reach and does not participate in the wrist (radiocarpal) joint[cite: 177].

inTextQuestions.question: Which carpal bone is the largest in the carpus, and which is the most commonly fractured?
inTextQuestions.answer: The capitate is the largest carpal bone[cite: 190], and the scaphoid is the most commonly fractured[cite: 191].

saqs.question: State the three main functions of the clavicle and identify the neurovascular structures passing behind its medial third.
saqs.answer: The clavicle transmits forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, acts as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (principally supported by trapezius), and provides muscle attachments[cite: 168]. Behind its medial third pass the third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus, separated only by the subclavius muscle[cite: 167].

saqs.question: Match each humeral fracture site to the nerve most likely to be injured: surgical neck, radial groove, distal humerus, and medial epicondyle.
saqs.answer: Surgical neck fracture injures the axillary nerve; radial groove (midshaft) fracture injures the radial nerve; distal humerus fracture injures the median nerve; and medial epicondyle fracture injures the ulnar nerve[cite: 174].

saqs.question: Differentiate between a Colles' fracture, Smith's fracture, Galeazzi fracture, and Monteggia fracture.
saqs.answer: A Colles' fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal (posterior) displacement (dinner fork deformity)[cite: 187]; a Smith's fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar (ventral) displacement[cite: 187]; a Galeazzi fracture is a radius fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation[cite: 187]; and a Monteggia fracture is a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head[cite: 187].

saqs.question: Why is a fracture of the proximal radial shaft (proximal to pronator teres insertion) splinted in supination?
saqs.answer: When fractured proximal to the pronator teres insertion, the biceps supinates the proximal fragment while the pronator teres pronates the distal fragment; splinting the forearm in supination aligns the distal fragment with the supinated proximal end[cite: 182].

saqs.question: List the proximal and distal rows of carpal bones from lateral to medial, and explain why scaphoid fractures risk avascular necrosis.
saqs.answer: Proximal row (lateral to medial): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform[cite: 189]. Distal row (lateral to medial): trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate[cite: 190]. The scaphoid risks avascular necrosis because only one small artery enters the bone at the end closest to the thumb, so a fracture tearing this vessel cuts off blood supply to the lower half of the bone[cite: 192].
